title: How Much Earnest Money for a Wholesale Deal? A Practical Guide for Investors
excerpt: Knowing how much earnest money to put down on a wholesale deal can make or break your negotiation. This guide breaks down the numbers, the strategy, and what sellers actually expect.

sections.content: If you're new to wholesaling real estate, one of the first questions you'll face is: how much earnest money should I put down? It feels like a small detail, but it can determine whether a seller takes you seriously, whether your deal falls through, and how much of your own cash is at risk. The good news is that earnest money in wholesale deals is typically much lower than in traditional real estate transactions — if you know what you're doing.
What Is Earnest Money in a Wholesale Deal?

Earnest money is a deposit you put down when you sign a purchase contract with a seller. It signals that you're a serious buyer and gives the seller confidence that you won't just walk away without consequence. In a traditional home purchase, earnest money is often 1% to 3% of the purchase price. On a $300,000 home, that could be $3,000 to $9,000. In wholesaling, however, the rules are different — and a lot more flexible. If you're just getting started, the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) is a great place to build your foundation before diving into deal mechanics.
How Much Earnest Money Do Wholesalers Actually Put Down?

The honest answer is: as little as possible. Most experienced wholesalers put down anywhere from $100 to $1,000 in earnest money on a wholesale deal. Some put down as little as $10. That might sound shocking if you come from a traditional real estate background, but it's completely normal in the wholesale world — especially when dealing with motivated sellers who just want to close quickly.
Common Earnest Money Ranges by Seller Type

items: Motivated sellers (pre-foreclosure, probate, divorce): $100 to $500 is usually accepted without pushback
On-market or MLS properties: Sellers and agents often expect $1,000 to $5,000 to be competitive
Bank-owned or REO properties: May require $500 to $2,500 depending on the asset manager
Absentee landlord deals: $250 to $1,000 is the sweet spot in most cases
Competitive markets like Atlanta, Dallas, or Phoenix: Expect to go higher — sometimes $1,000 to $2,500 — to stand out

sections.content: Pro Tip: Always negotiate the earnest money amount just like you negotiate the purchase price. Most motivated sellers are far more focused on your closing timeline and their net proceeds than on how much you're putting in escrow up front. Start low and only go higher if you face pushback.
Why Wholesalers Keep Earnest Money Low

Wholesalers aren't buying the property — they're buying the right to assign the contract to an end buyer. That means you're only in the deal for a short window, usually 7 to 30 days. During that time, you're out finding a cash buyer or another investor. Tying up $5,000 across multiple deals simultaneously can drain your operating capital fast. Keeping earnest money at $100 to $500 per deal lets you run several contracts at once without breaking the bank.

There's also a risk management angle. If your due diligence reveals the deal doesn't work — maybe the repairs are worse than expected or your buyers pass — you want your exposure to be minimal. A solid contingency clause in your contract (like an inspection contingency or a financing contingency) can also protect you if you need to exit a deal without losing your deposit. If you're still learning how all these pieces fit together, check out this [Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/real-estate-investing-for-beginners) for a full breakdown.
How Market Conditions Affect Your Earnest Money Strategy

In slower markets, sellers are more flexible. You can often get away with $100 to $250 and a 30-day close window. In hot markets, competition changes the game entirely. If you're working deals in high-demand metros, you may need to raise your earnest money to compete. For example, wholesalers working the [Atlanta market](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga) or the [Dallas–Fort Worth area](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx) often report that sellers — especially those who've been approached by multiple wholesalers — expect at least $500 to $1,000. In [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), where investor activity is intense, some wholesalers go up to $2,000 to make their offer feel more credible.

"In wholesale deals, earnest money isn't about the dollar amount — it's about showing the seller you have skin in the game. Even $500 signals commitment. The real negotiation is in the price and the timeline." — Experienced real estate wholesaler
Step-by-Step: What to Do With Earnest Money on Your Next Deal
1. Start Your Offer Low

When you submit your purchase agreement, start with $100 to $500 as your earnest money deposit. Don't volunteer a higher number unless the seller or their agent asks. Most motivated sellers won't negotiate this point at all — they care more about your offer price and how quickly you can close.
2. Use a Title Company or Escrow to Hold the Deposit

Never hand cash directly to a seller. Always have your earnest money held by a neutral third party — a title company, an escrow company, or a real estate attorney. This protects both parties and keeps everything clean and legally sound. It also builds seller trust because they know the money is real and secured.
3. Protect Yourself With Contingencies

Your contract should include contingencies that let you exit the deal and recover your deposit if something goes wrong. An inspection contingency is the most common. Some wholesalers use a broad 'due diligence' contingency that gives them a window to back out for any reason. Make sure your attorney reviews your contract language before you sign anything.
4. Know Your Numbers Before You Sign

Before you put any money on the table, you need to know if the deal actually makes sense. Run your numbers using the free [Wholesale Deal Calculator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to figure out your maximum allowable offer, your potential assignment fee, and your buyer's likely profit margin. If the deal doesn't pencil out, no amount of earnest money negotiation will save it.
When You Might Need to Go Higher

items: The seller has been burned by a wholesaler who backed out before — they'll want more skin in the game from you
You're working with a real estate agent who is representing the seller and pushing for a larger deposit
The deal is on the MLS and other buyers are submitting offers with standard earnest money amounts
You're dealing with an estate or probate property where the executor needs to show the court a legitimate contract
You've already built a relationship with this seller and want to lock the deal tight before a competitor swoops in

sections.content: Pro Tip: If a seller pushes back on your low earnest money offer, try this reframe: 'I understand your concern. I close fast and in cash — my buyers are ready. The earnest money is low, but you'll have a signed purchase agreement and a firm close date within the week.' Speed and certainty often matter more to a motivated seller than deposit size.
The Bottom Line on Earnest Money for Wholesale Deals

For most wholesale deals, $100 to $1,000 is the standard range. Motivated sellers on off-market deals are usually comfortable with $100 to $500. On-market or competitive deals may require $1,000 or more to be taken seriously. The key is to protect your capital, use solid contract contingencies, and always run your numbers before you commit. Earnest money is a signal of intent — not a down payment — and savvy wholesalers treat it that way.
